title: "221B Baker Street" and "221 Baker Street" extract to the same house number
assumption: Pulling the leading digits off an address line gives you a unique house-number key.

input.display: "221B Baker Street" vs "221 Baker Street"; "12\u00bd Main Street" vs "12 Main Street"
input.description: A geocoding or dedup step that extracts 'the house number' from an address line with a leading-digits regex, to compare or key addresses.

what_goes_wrong: Two genuinely different addresses — a subdivided unit "221B" and the plain "221" — collapse to the identical extracted number "221", silently merging two different physical locations in any system that keys on the extracted value.
why: A leading-digit regex like ^(\d+) stops at the first non-digit character, so it captures only "221" and discards the trailing letter suffix "B" — which is not decoration: it typically marks a separate property created by subdividing or infilling, and is what distinguishes it from plain 221. The same problem affects fractional house numbers like "12½", where the regex captures "12" and silently drops the ½ that distinguishes it from plain "12".
affects: any 'extract leading digits as the house number' parser

repros.expected_output:
221B Baker Street -> 221
221 Baker Street -> 221
12½ Main Street -> 12
12 Main Street -> 12

221B Baker Street -> 221
221 Baker Street -> 221
12½ Main Street -> 12
12 Main Street -> 12

fix: Keep the full house-number token, including any letter suffix or fraction, as the key, instead of truncating to the leading digits; treat "221" and "221B" as different addresses unless you've confirmed otherwise.

sources.title: Michael Tandy: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Addresses

test_cases.note: These are two different addresses; your house-number extraction should not treat them as the same key.
